facts.fact: Micro Center now requires RTX 5090 buyers to show photo ID and sign a no-export pledge, as U.S. authorities have only recently begun seriously cracking down on GPU smuggling.
facts.why: Retail enforcement of existing controls on a consumer card; says nothing about a U.S. or Chinese decision on data-center Blackwell exports.

why: The articles repeat guidance, smuggling and export-control facts already in the request; nothing new on a U.S. Blackwell authorization or a Chinese decision.

facts.fact: Nvidia's inventory rose to $31.58bn from $21.40bn at fiscal year-end and receivables to $63.06bn from $38.47bn.
facts.why: Shows a supply build-up but cannot pull commitments below $125bn when $279bn is already disclosed.

facts.fact: Nvidia raised the 128GB DGX Spark price to $6,950 on Oct 2 and launched a half-memory model to cut bill-of-materials cost, citing the memory shortage.
facts.why: Confirms rising memory costs that keep dollar commitments high; the answer already sits in the top rung.

facts.fact: HBM needs about three times the wafer capacity of standard DRAM and memory makers compete for limited EUV tools, keeping HBM supply tight.
facts.why: Supports sustained large memory commitments; same top-rung answer.

why: Every new fact points the same way as the $279bn disclosure; none suggests fiscal-year-end commitments below $125bn.

facts.fact: Broadcom's fiscal Q2 AI semiconductor revenue was $10.8bn, up 143% year over year, and it guided Q3 to $16.0bn (more than 200% growth, per A2).
facts.why: One custom-chip supplier's AI revenue run rate alone implies roughly $40bn or more in calendar 2026, against the below-$40bn answer.

facts.fact: Amazon has disclosed Trainium is a multi-billion-dollar business; Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta all fund custom chips (Trainium, TPU, Maia, MTIA), with Trainium and TPU volumes rising.
facts.why: Adds custom-chip spending beyond Broadcom's customers; unquantified alone, but pushes the total higher.

facts.fact: Broadcom makes custom AI chips for Alphabet (TPU), Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI, with production for the latter three ramping late 2026 into 2027.
facts.why: Broader customer base, but new ramps fall mostly in 2027, so the 2026 effect is modest.

facts.fact: Google guided 2026 capex up to $190bn with a Cloud backlog near $460bn, strengthening its in-house TPU case.
facts.why: A larger budget at the main TPU buyer makes sizable custom-silicon spending more plausible; no ASIC figure given.

facts.fact: Bloomberg Intelligence forecasts a 27% CAGR for custom ASICs through 2033 versus 16% for AI accelerators.
facts.why: A growth rate without a base level cannot place 2026 spending on the ladder.

why: The request holds no spending figure; Broadcom's reported and guided AI revenue alone likely lifts 2026 custom-silicon spending above $40bn, moving the answer up.

facts.fact: Nvidia already guarantees a minimum revenue level on part of NeoCloud facilities' capacity and takes a share of earnings above that level.
facts.why: Shows Nvidia already writes customer guarantees, supporting yes, though it is not a residual-value guarantee.

facts.fact: Nvidia reported guarantee obligations capped at $108.5bn for AI cloud and data center partners.
facts.why: If any of this is a residual-value guarantee, yes may already hold; the article does not say what the guarantees cover.

facts.fact: Morningstar says material use of residual-value guarantees or credit enhancements would weaken Nvidia's credit assessment by increasing claims on liquidity in a downturn.
facts.why: A credit cost gives Nvidia reason to shrink or avoid the guarantee, slightly weakening the yes answer.

facts.fact: Bond investors in Amazon's chip SPV expect investment-grade ratings based on Amazon's AA credit rather than on the hardware's residual value.
facts.why: Shows lenders can rely on lessee credit instead of residual values; bears only weakly on Nvidia's guarantee.

why: New facts are indirect and cut both ways; none shows the guarantee signed, withdrawn or abandoned, so yes stands at similar strength.

facts.fact: Amazon enlarged its March bond to about $50bn from $37bn, issued another $25bn in July, and had to pay higher yields on some longer-dated debt.
facts.why: Shows funding strain and capacity, but Amazon's roughly $220bn 2026 plan is already in the request.

facts.fact: Broadcom expects about $115bn of AI semiconductor revenue in 2027, doubling to $230bn in 2028.
facts.why: Concerns 2027-28 supplier revenue, not calendar-2026 hyperscaler capex.

facts.fact: Analysts estimate Nvidia's revenue at $411bn this year, about 40% of a roughly $1tn total AI spend.
facts.why: Consistent with the roughly $800bn big-five figure already shown; adds no big-five capex number.

facts.fact: Tencent reportedly signed a five-year deal with Oracle worth about $7bn for access to roughly 100,000 advanced AI chips.
facts.why: Small and spread over five years; no measurable effect on 2026 big-five capex.

why: Articles repeat the $800bn estimate and Amazon and Meta figures already shown; nothing new quantifies 2026 big-five capex outside $750-850bn.

facts.fact: Amazon raised its 2026 capex projection to about $220bn from $200bn, driven mainly by rising memory prices for AI servers.
facts.why: A higher 2026 base and cost inflation support the $1.3tn path, perhaps toward the upper half of the band.

facts.fact: Nvidia's revenue per gigawatt rises from $18bn for Hopper to $25bn for Blackwell and $40bn for Vera Rubin, now in full production.
facts.why: More dollars per gigawatt raises spending per unit of capacity built in 2027, supporting the projection.

facts.fact: Huang reaffirmed that data-center capex will reach $3-4tn a year by 2030; total 2026 AI spending including non-big-five buyers may reach $1tn.
facts.why: A long-range global figure implies strong growth but no specific 2027 big-five number.

facts.fact: Amazon's $8bn chip sale-leaseback could, if completed, prompt similar asset-securitization moves by other big tech companies.
facts.why: If widely adopted, some hardware spending may show as leases rather than reported capex; scale unknown.

facts.fact: Lenders question whether chips are reliable collateral and some seek broader guarantees; higher financing costs or stricter terms could slow data-center expansion.
facts.why: An unquantified downside risk to reaching $1.3tn; same band, lower confidence.

why: New facts mostly support continued growth, with financing and off-balance-sheet risks; none quantifies 2027 big-five capex away from about $1.3tn.
